question: Should the change described in scenario.md ship?

findings.claim: The one-time UPDATE copy of fullname into display_name does not capture writes made to fullname during the migration window, and a partial failure of the unprotected UPDATE on 4M rows followed by an unconditional DROP COLUMN can permanently destroy un-migrated data.
findings.evidence: Migration: `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name TEXT; UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname; ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname;` — the UPDATE runs outside a transaction on a 4 million row table, and the script proceeds to DROP COLUMN fullname regardless of whether the UPDATE fully/correctly completed.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the backfill in a transaction (or batched transactions with verification), add a count/checksum check that display_name is fully populated before dropping fullname, and keep writes dual-targeted (or use a trigger) during the transition window so concurrent updates to fullname are not lost.

findings.claim: There is no down-migration and the schema/app-code cutover happens in a single deploy, making the change irreversible and unsafe for rolling deployments.
findings.evidence: Scenario states: 'There is no down-migration' and 'Application code is updated in the same deploy to read and write display_name' with fullname dropped in the same script. During a rolling deploy, old app instances still expecting fullname will break the moment the column is dropped, and rolling back the app deploy cannot restore fullname without a backup/down-migration.
findings.suggestion: Use an expand/contract pattern: ship the add-column + backfill + dual-write first, deploy app code that can read either column, verify in production, and only drop fullname in a later, separate, easily-abortable migration. Provide a tested down-migration or documented restore-from-backup procedure before the DROP COLUMN step ships.

findings.claim: Concurrent writes to fullname during the migration window (between the UPDATE copy and the app/schema cutover) are silently lost.
findings.evidence: The UPDATE is a single point-in-time copy with no mechanism (trigger, dual-write, or lock) to capture subsequent writes to fullname before DROP COLUMN fullname executes; on a 4M-row production table this window can be long and concurrent profile edits are likely.
findings.suggestion: Add a trigger or dual-write logic to keep display_name and fullname in sync for the duration of the transition, or run the backfill as the very last step immediately before cutover with writes blocked/queued.

findings.claim: An unrelated optional `pronunciation` column is bundled into an already high-risk migration PR, increasing review surface and blast radius for no stated need.
findings.evidence: Scenario: 'The ticket asked only for the rename, but the PR also adds an optional pronunciation column "while we're here."'
findings.suggestion: Split the pronunciation column into its own PR/migration so the risky rename can be reviewed, tested, and rolled back independently.

investigate.what: Whether the migration runner wraps the entire script in an implicit transaction, and what happens to already-applied migration state if the process is killed mid-UPDATE.
investigate.why: Determines actual blast radius of a partial-failure scenario; could not be verified from the scenario text alone.
tools: Running the migration against a staging DB

investigate.what: The deployment topology (single-instance vs rolling/blue-green) and how long the dual-version window lasts.
investigate.why: Determines how severe the old-code/new-schema mismatch window is in practice.

conditions: Decouple the destructive step: deploy app code that can read/write display_name while fullname still exists (dual-write or fallback), then drop fullname only after confirming the new code path works in production. Don't ship the ADD+COPY+DROP as one irreversible migration bundled with the app cutover.

Run the backfill UPDATE in batches (or at least wrap row-range chunks in short transactions) instead of a single unbounded UPDATE outside a transaction on a 4M-row table, to avoid long locks/replication lag.
Drop the 'pronunciation' column addition from this PR; ship it separately if/when there's an actual ticket or use case for it.

findings.claim: If anything goes wrong after deploy, there is no quick, safe way back: the column is dropped irrecoverably and app code is already pointed at the new column in the same release.
findings.evidence: Migration has 'no down-migration' and does ADD -> COPY -> DROP of fullname in one shot, with application code switched to display_name in the same deploy.
findings.suggestion: Split into add-column / dual-read-write / verify / drop-column as separate deploys, so a bad deploy can be rolled back by reverting app code without needing the dropped column back.

findings.claim: The PR adds an unrelated 'pronunciation' column that the ticket never asked for.
findings.evidence: Scenario states: 'The ticket asked only for the rename, but the PR also adds an optional pronunciation column "while we're here".'
findings.suggestion: Ship the rename alone; file the pronunciation column as its own ticket/PR.

findings.claim: No concrete user-facing benefit is named for this change beyond an internal field rename; users see the same name, just under a renamed column.
findings.evidence: The change is described purely as a schema rename ('rename users.fullname to users.display_name') with application code updated to match; no new capability or visible fix is described.
findings.suggestion: If this rename unblocks a planned feature (e.g., supporting display names distinct from legal names), state that explicitly and ship it in the same release as that feature so the value lands now, not later.

investigate.what: Whether the production database/ORM enforces a maintenance window or has replicas sensitive to long-running unbatched UPDATEs on a 4M-row table.
investigate.why: An unbatched UPDATE outside a transaction on a large table can cause replication lag or lock contention that affects live users; this can only be confirmed by running/profiling the migration against a prod-like dataset.
tools: staging environment with representative data volume
